projects.name: Engineering OS
projects.summary: One command gives Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any other agent the same vetted skills, safety guards and playbooks in every project you open, and tells you when a new version ships.

Guards that block destructive commands and stop secrets landing in source
Detects the stack and loads the matching playbook on its own
Grades your agent setup and fires fake attacks at your guards

hi.tagline: कोडिंग एजेंट्स के लिए ऑपरेटिंग सिस्टम
hi.summary: एक कमांड से Claude Code, Codex, Cursor या किसी भी दूसरे एजेंट को हर प्रोजेक्ट में वही जाँची-परखी स्किल्स, सेफ़्टी गार्ड और प्लेबुक मिलती हैं, और नया वर्ज़न आने पर यह आपको बता देता है।
capabilities: एक ही कमांड से प्लगइन, गार्ड, काम के नियम और जाँची-परखी स्किल्स इंस्टॉल
गार्ड, जो विनाशकारी कमांड रोकते हैं और सीक्रेट्स को सोर्स कोड में जाने नहीं देते
स्टैक पहचानकर सही प्लेबुक अपने-आप लोड करता है
आपके एजेंट सेटअप को ग्रेड देता है और आपके गार्ड्स पर नकली हमले करता है
नई स्किल्स ढूँढता है, जाँचता है और आपकी हर मशीन पर इंस्टॉल करता है

projects.why:
Every new project, I was setting up my coding agent from scratch: the same skills, the same rules, the same “please don’t force-push to main”. And every agent keeps them somewhere different.

So I put it all in one harness that installs with a single command. It only takes skills from official vendors or well-known authors, it guards the commands that can hurt you, and it loads the right playbook for the stack it finds. Then I pointed a red team at my own guards. It found 13 holes in version 0.5.0, which is why the red team now ships with it.
howItWorks: The installer clones the repo to ~/engineering-os, links the plugin and puts the eos command on your PATH. The whole script sits inside one main() function, so bash reads all of it before running anything from a curl pipe.

Skills come from a registry of 161: 84 installed by default and 77 on demand, so the agent isn’t flooded. To get in, a skill needs an official vendor or a well-known author, at least 1,000 installs, and no install-time scripts.
When a session starts, a hook detects the project’s stack and routes the agent to the matching playbook.

Before every shell command, a guard sorts it. Some are blocked outright (rm -rf ~, mkfs, a fork bomb). Others need your yes: force-push, git reset --hard, DROP TABLE, curl | sh, production deploys. A second guard stops secrets from being written into source files.
eos redteam fires 51 fake attacks and 35 everyday commands at your own guards without running any of them, and scores what got through.
Whatever the guards catch is logged locally with secrets redacted. Nothing is uploaded.

projects.why:
I run Claude Code, Codex and Cursor side by side, usually across a few terminal tabs. A lot of my time was going to tab-hunting: which one finished, which one is stuck waiting for me to approve something.

The MacBook notch was just sitting there. So I turned it into a status bar for my agents. I can see who is working, approve a permission request with ⌘Y, and get back to what I was doing. Everything runs on my Mac. No accounts, no API keys, no telemetry.
howItWorks: The app runs a small local server on 127.0.0.1:7433. It turns each agent’s signals into one shared set of events, keeps state per session and streams it to the island.
For Claude Code and Cursor it merges hooks into their settings files. It never removes your own hooks, writes a timestamped backup first, and skips any file it can’t parse.
Claude’s events go through a small bridge script instead of an HTTP hook. If the app is closed, an HTTP hook would show an error on every call; the script fails quietly.
Permission requests are held open for up to 120 seconds, so you can answer them from the notch. “Always allow” writes the same rule as Claude Code’s own “don’t ask again”.
Codex is read-only: the app tails its session logs.
Every request to the local server needs a token. The Ask bar runs on Apple’s on-device model, which only ever sees one line per session.

projects.why:
On a developer’s Mac, the disk rarely fills up with your own files. It fills up with node_modules from forgotten projects, Xcode DerivedData, Electron caches and scratch files left behind by coding agents. Often tens of gigabytes, and all of it can be rebuilt.

General cleaners either miss that kind of junk or delete things you can’t get back. So I built purge around one rule: it deletes only what you leave checked, and anything risky starts unchecked. No telemetry, no network calls, zero runtime dependencies.
howItWorks: One scan covers build output, package caches, Xcode, Electron apps, coding agents, browsers, editors, logs, orphans and heavy files. Each group has its own scanner.
Every row passes a chain of guards: home, your keep list, danger paths, cloud-sync folders (iCloud, Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive), fragile paths, symlinks, volumes and git.
The git guard asks git which paths are ignored, in one batched call per repo with a 10-second timeout. If git fails, it leaves those rows unchecked. Failing toward caution is deliberate.
Sizes come from disk blocks, not file size, so iCloud placeholders that aren’t really on disk don’t count as space you’d get back.
Right before deleting, every guard runs again. Trash mode moves files to ~/.Trash, and every run writes a manifest, so purge undo can put things back.
Only one file in the codebase is allowed to delete anything. CI enforces that, and fails the build if a runtime dependency ever sneaks in.

projects.why:
Arthion was my experiment in a financial research agent: ask about a company or a market, and get an answer grounded in real financial data and charts instead of a model’s memory.

I’m no longer developing it, but it taught me a lot about splitting fast chat from slow, long-running agent work.
howItWorks: Chat streams through the Vercel AI SDK, with tools for financial data and charts and a web search fallback. The number of agent steps is capped.
There are two agents: one for financial questions and one for markets.
Long-running research tasks go onto a Redis-backed queue and run on a separate worker service. They report progress and can be cancelled.
A guardrail wraps the model and keeps conversations on finance.
Chat history and a knowledge base are embedded, so the agent can recall relevant context by similarity.

projects.name: God of Debugger
projects.summary: Debug by disproving. One slash command turns a bug report into a falsification protocol, and a fix is proposed only when exactly one hypothesis is left standing.
capabilities: Bootstraps a deterministic repro before hypothesising
Generates competing primary and adversarial hypotheses
One falsification experiment per hypothesis, run by parallel subagents
Survival table scoring each hypothesis killed, survived, or inconclusive
Promotes surviving experiments into permanent regression tests

hi.tagline: Claude Code के लिए डीबगिंग प्लगइन
hi.summary: ग़लत साबित करके डीबग करें। एक स्लैश कमांड बग रिपोर्ट को फ़ॉल्सिफ़िकेशन प्रोटोकॉल में बदल देता है, और फ़िक्स तभी सुझाया जाता है जब सिर्फ़ एक हाइपोथीसिस बची रह जाए।
capabilities: हाइपोथीसिस बनाने से पहले एक डिटर्मिनिस्टिक रिप्रो तैयार करता है
आपस में टकराती प्राइमरी और एडवर्सेरियल हाइपोथीसिस बनाता है
हर हाइपोथीसिस के लिए एक फ़ॉल्सिफ़िकेशन एक्सपेरिमेंट, जिन्हें पैरेलल सबएजेंट चलाते हैं
सर्वाइवल टेबल, जो हर हाइपोथीसिस को ख़ारिज, बची हुई या अनिर्णीत आँकती है
बचे हुए एक्सपेरिमेंट को स्थायी रिग्रेशन टेस्ट में बदल देता है

projects.why:
Coding agents debug the way tired people do: they latch onto the first plausible cause and ship a fix. Sometimes it’s right. Often it just moves the bug.

God of Debugger makes the agent work like a scientist instead. It writes down several competing explanations, tries to kill each one with an experiment, and is only allowed to fix the bug when exactly one explanation survives.
howItWorks: /god-of-debugger:go reproduces the bug, narrows it to 2–5 files, then writes 5–8 hypotheses that cover at least 4 of 7 causes: data, control flow, concurrency, config, dependencies, environment and contracts.
An adversary subagent adds 2–3 more hypotheses in the categories the first list missed, including “the premise is wrong”.
Each hypothesis gets one experiment, with its kill and survive conditions written down before it runs. Runners can’t rewrite them after seeing the output.
One runner per hypothesis works in parallel and sees only its own hypothesis and files. Each returns killed, survived or inconclusive.
A fix is allowed only when exactly one hypothesis survives, and a hook enforces it: until then, edits to production files are blocked.
The surviving experiment becomes a regression test that fails before the fix and passes after it.
stack: Claude Code plugins, subagents and hooks

hi.summary: रियल-टाइम प्रीव्यू, सुरक्षित डॉक्यूमेंट शेयरिंग और एन्क्रिप्शन एट रेस्ट वाला मार्कडाउन एडिटर। डेवलपर्स और लेखकों के लिए मुफ़्त।

एन्क्रिप्शन एट रेस्ट
लिखने के लिए AI इंटीग्रेशन

projects.why:
I write a lot of Markdown, and more and more of it comes out of AI assistants. Getting it from a chat window into something I can share always meant copy, paste and fix the formatting.

Marcko is a Markdown editor built for that. It renders what developers actually write, like math, diagrams and live code, and it gives AI assistants a way to publish straight into your library.
howItWorks: A live editor and preview with GitHub-flavoured Markdown, math, syntax highlighting and Mermaid diagrams.
HTML, CSS and JavaScript code blocks run in a sandboxed iframe, so a snippet can be tried right in the document.
Documents can be shared as public or private. Content is encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, and every save keeps a version.
The marcko-mcp server gives AI clients like Claude Code a publish_to_marcko tool, so an assistant can publish a document without any copy-paste.
API keys are stored only as a SHA-256 hash plus their last four characters, and compared in constant time.

hi.summary: Next.js और OpenAI Agents SDK पर बने, प्रोडक्शन के लिए तैयार एजेंट ऐप्स का टेम्पलेट — मॉड्यूलर टूल स्ट्रक्चर और डिप्लॉयमेंट तक के तेज़ रास्ते के साथ।
capabilities: प्रोडक्शन के लिए तैयार Next.js इंटीग्रेशन
OpenAI Agents SDK सपोर्ट
मॉड्यूलर टूल और एजेंट स्ट्रक्चर

projects.why:
Every agent project I started began with the same hour of setup: Next.js, the OpenAI Agents SDK, a streaming API route, input validation, sessions. So I turned that hour into one command.

You get a working agent app with typed tools, streaming and a choice of two templates, ready to change into whatever you’re building.
howItWorks: The CLI copies one of two templates: a single agent with tools, or a triage agent that hands off to specialists. It sets up your package manager of choice (npm, pnpm, yarn or bun) and runs git init.
The /api/agent route returns plain JSON, or a stream of server-sent events, and tells the UI which agent is active after a handoff.
Every request is validated with a strict Zod schema: messages up to 4,000 characters, between 1 and 20 agent turns.
Server sessions live in memory with a 30-minute timeout and a cap of 200, both configurable.
The default model is gpt-5-mini, and one environment variable changes it.

projects.why: Most people with a spreadsheet have a question about it, not a chart in mind. Aarekhit lets you upload your data and ask in plain English, and it picks and draws the chart for you.
howItWorks: Upload a CSV or Excel file (up to 10 MB) and you get a preview of the first rows.
Each prompt is classified as a new chart or a follow-up question about the current one. If the classifier is unavailable, simple local scoring takes over.
The model, Gemini or OpenAI, which you can choose, returns a chart spec. Model output is repaired in stages if it isn’t valid JSON, with up to three retries.
Charts render with Plotly: bar, line, pie, scatter, area, radar, funnel, sunburst, sankey, treemap and tables.
A Deep Research mode pulls in web sources and adds them to the analysis.

projects.why: Notex is an AI note-taking app I built to find out what an assistant inside your notes should actually do. Search that understands meaning, writing help that stays out of the way, and notes you can listen to.
howItWorks: Sign-in is passwordless, by a one-time code over email or phone, through Appwrite.
Semantic search runs entirely in your browser: TensorFlow.js embeds your query and notes with the Universal Sentence Encoder and ranks them by cosine similarity. No embedding API is involved.
Around a dozen AI actions (outline, improve, summarise, tags, translate, mind map and more) each use their own Gemini prompt and temperature.
The editor autosaves after three seconds of quiet and previews Markdown as you type.
You can dictate with the Web Speech API and have notes read back to you.

projects.why: A PDF is a fine way to store a book and a poor way to read one. Readany turns a PDF into something that feels like a book, with pages you actually turn.
howItWorks: You upload a PDF. pdf.js renders each page to an image in the browser, with a progress bar as it goes.
Pages are pre-rendered at twice the resolution, so the page-flip animation stays smooth.
The pages are bound between a generated front and back cover, with a drawn spine.
Read with the arrow keys, zoom from half size to double, or go fullscreen.
Three themes (light, dark and warm paper) and three reading modes (normal, high contrast and sepia).
